newsitem.title: GERMANY: Serbs, Albanians to seek Kosovo solution in Munich.
newsitem.headline: Serbs, Albanians to seek Kosovo solution in Munich.

text.p: Serbian government officials meet opposition members and ethnic Albanians on Tuesday in Munich to discuss the future status of Serbia's Albanian-majority province of Kosovo, the talks' organiser said on Monday.

The meeting, aimed at preparing an agenda for official talks, comes days after an assassination attempt on a prominent Serb in Kosovo which has again focused attention on government and opposition attitudes to the polticially sensitive region, regarded by Serb nationalists as the cradle of their culture .

Belgrade revoked Kosovo's regional autonomy in 1989, accusing the 90 percent ethnic Albanian majority of wanting to secede. But the Serbian opposition, many of whose figures are strong nationalists, have not made their position on Kosovo clear.

"The key problem for democracy in Serbia is Kosovo. The Serbian opposition cannot say they have a democracy without solving the Kosovo problem," talks' organiser Cornelius Ochmann of the Bertelsmann Foundation told Reuters.
At the one-day meeting at Munich University, delegates will discuss three blueprints for Kosovo's future status: as an autonomous region, autonomous republic or independent state.

Ochmann said some dozen delegates would take part, including a Serbian government adviser, an opposition expert on minorities and the ethnic Albanian publisher of an Albanian-language newspaper in Kosovo.
Western experts from Germany and other European Union states will also be there, said Ochmann. The foundation is a non profit-making body set up by the Bertelsmann media group.
The first round of unofficial talks was held on the Greek island of Rhodes last September. The results of this second round will be made public in April and official talks are expected to follow.

Ochmann said a key difference since the first meeting was that the Serbian opposition coalition Zajedno (Together), which has kept up protests since the authorities' annulment of municipal elections last November, was stronger now.
"The position of (opposition leaders Vuk) Draskovic and (Zoran) Djindjic on Kosovo used to be rather ambiguous," said Ochmann. "We want to see if they have clarifed their stance."
Zajedno's campaign to democratise Serbia has been jolted by a car bomb attack last week on the Serb rector of the university in Pristina, Kosovo's main city.
The attack prompted accusations from Serb authorities in Kosovo that Serbian opposition members had plotted the attack with ethnic Albanian separatists.
Albanian media published a claim of responsibility from the radical Liberation Army of Kosovo.

The Serbian opposition denied involvement, and said they feared the ruling Socialists would try to exploit the bombing to discredit a campaign of pro-democracy protests against the authorities' annulment of local elections last November.
